lessons.title: Indexing and slicing
lessons.summary: Every character in a string has a position — how to grab one, or a section.
lessons.notes:
A **string** is a sequence of characters. Each character has a position, called an **index**, starting at 0 (not 1).

```python
word = "Python"
print(word[0])    # P - the first character
print(word[-1])   # n - the last character, counting from the end
print(len(word))  # 6 - how many characters in total
```

A **slice** takes a section of a string: `word[start:end]` gives everything from `start` up to (but not including) `end`.

```python
print(word[0:3])  # Pyt
print(word[2:])   # thon - leaving off the end means "to the end"
print(word[:2])   # Py - leaving off the start means "from the start"
```

OCR's pseudocode calls this `SUBSTRING` or `MID` — a Python slice does the same job.
lessons.worked_example_note: Indexing starts at 0, so name[0] is the first letter, not name[1]. In name[0:3], index 3 itself is not included — you get exactly 3 characters.

lessons.title: String methods and building strings
lessons.summary: upper(), lower(), strip(), replace(), split() and checking with in.
lessons.notes:
Python strings come with useful built-in methods:

| Method | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.upper()` | capital letters | `"hi".upper()` → `"HI"` |
| `.lower()` | lower-case letters | `"HI".lower()` → `"hi"` |
| `.strip()` | removes spaces from each end | `" hi ".strip()` → `"hi"` |
| `.replace(a, b)` | swaps every `a` for `b` | `"cat".replace("c", "b")` → `"bat"` |
| `.split()` | splits into a list of words | `"a b c".split()` → `["a", "b", "c"]` |

A method doesn't change the original string — it hands back a **new** one, so you usually need to store the result: `name = name.strip()`.

Use `in` to check whether one string appears inside another: `"cat" in "concatenate"` is `True`.

Join text and variables together with an f-string: `f"Hello {name}"`.
lessons.worked_example_note: Methods can be chained: .strip() runs first, then .lower() runs on its result. The original text variable is left unchanged — clean is a separate new string.

lessons.title: Exam-style string problems
lessons.summary: Combining checks and transformations to validate or build text.
lessons.notes:
String questions usually combine a few of these ideas:

1. **Read** — get the text with `input()`
2. **Check** — inspect it (length, whether it contains something, comparing characters)
3. **Transform** — build a new string (slicing, methods, joining pieces together)
4. **Report** — print the result in the format asked for

A common OCR-style task is validation: checking a piece of text meets some rules before accepting it. It's the same shape as the number validation from the Iteration topic — you're just checking a property of text (like its length) instead of whether a number is in range.
lessons.worked_example_note: len() counts every character, including spaces. This is exactly the same validation shape you've already used for numbers, just checking a different property.

quiz.question: For word = "Python", what does word[0] give you?
quiz.explanation: Indexing starts at 0, so word[0] is the first character.

quiz.question: What does word[-1] give you?
quiz.explanation: Negative indices count from the end; -1 is always the last character, whatever the string's length.

quiz.question: For word = "Python", what does word[0:3] give you?
quiz.explanation: Slicing word[0:3] takes the characters at index 0, 1 and 2 - the end index (3) itself is not included.

quiz.question: What does "hi".upper() return?
quiz.explanation: upper() converts every letter in the string to a capital letter.

quiz.question: Which method removes extra spaces from the start and end of a string?
quiz.explanation: strip() removes whitespace from both ends, leaving the middle of the string untouched.

quiz.question: What does "cat" in "concatenate" evaluate to?
quiz.explanation: in checks whether one string appears anywhere inside another - "concatenate" contains "cat".

quiz.question: What does len("hello world") return?
quiz.explanation: len() counts every character including the space, so "hello world" has 11 characters.

quiz.question: What does "banana".count("a") return?
quiz.explanation: count() tallies how many times the given character appears - "a" appears 3 times in "banana".

quiz.question: "Ada Lovelace".split() gives which of these?
quiz.explanation: split() with no arguments splits on whitespace, giving a list of the individual words.

tasks.title: First letter
tasks.brief:
Read a word. Print its first character.

For example, hello prints h.
hints: The first character of a string is always at index 0.
word = input(), then print(word[0])

tasks.title: Last letter
tasks.brief:
Read a word. Print its last character.

For example, hello prints o.
hints: Index -1 always means "the last character", however long the word is - you don't need to work out the length first.
word = input(), then print(word[-1])

tasks.title: String length
tasks.brief: Read a word. Print how many characters it has.
hints: len() works on strings the same way it works on lists.
word = input(), then print(len(word))

tasks.title: First three letters
tasks.brief:
Read a word (it will always be at least 3 characters long). Print its first three characters using slicing.

For example, Python prints Pyt.
hints: A slice from the start up to index 3 gives exactly the first 3 characters.
word = input(), then print(word[0:3])

tasks.title: Middle letter
tasks.brief:
Read a word with an odd number of characters (always odd). Print the character exactly in the middle.

For example, radar has 5 letters — its middle letter is d (index 2, with two letters before it and two after).
hints: This is the same idea as finding the middle item of an odd-length list: the middle index is len(word) // 2.
word = input(), then print(word[len(word) // 2])

tasks.title: Shout it
tasks.brief:
Read a line of text. Print it in capital letters.

For example, hello prints HELLO.
hints: text = input(), then print(text.upper())

tasks.title: Clean whitespace
tasks.brief: Read a line of text that may have extra spaces at the start or end. Print it with those spaces removed.
hints: text = input(), then print(text.strip())

tasks.title: Replace a word
tasks.brief:
Read a sentence. Replace every occurrence of the word cat with dog. Print the result.

For example, I have a cat prints I have a dog.
hints: text = input(), then print(text.replace("cat", "dog"))

tasks.title: Contains check
tasks.brief: Read a word, then a single letter, on separate lines. Print True if the letter appears inside the word, otherwise print False.
hints: word = input(), letter = input(), then print(letter in word)

tasks.title: Title case by hand
tasks.brief:
Read a word, always entirely lowercase. Print it with just the first letter capitalized and the rest unchanged — but without using Python's built-in .capitalize() or .title() methods. Build the result yourself using slicing and .upper().

For example, python prints Python.
hints: Split the word into two pieces: the first character (uppercased) and everything after it (unchanged), then join them back together.
word = input(), then print(word[0].upper() + word[1:])

tasks.title: Username length check
tasks.brief: Read a username. Print Valid if it is at least 5 characters long. Otherwise print Too short.
hints: Compare len(username) against 5, the same shape as the numeric range checks from Iteration.
username = input(), if len(username) >= 5: print("Valid"), else: print("Too short")

tasks.title: Count a letter
tasks.brief:
Read a word, then a single letter, on separate lines. Count how many times that letter appears in the word (this is case sensitive). Print the count.

For example, banana with the letter a gives 3.
hints: Python's .count() method does exactly this for you.
word = input(), letter = input(), then print(word.count(letter))

tasks.title: First and last match
tasks.brief:
Read a word. Print Match if its first and last characters are the same letter. Otherwise print No match.

For example, noon prints Match (n at both ends). cat prints No match.
hints: Compare word[0] with word[-1].
word = input(), print("Match") if word[0] == word[-1] else print("No match")

tasks.title: Initials
tasks.brief:
Read a person's full name as one line: a first name then a surname, separated by a single space. Print their initials, in the format `<first initial>.<last initial>.` — each initial followed by a full stop, no spaces.

For example, Ada Lovelace prints A.L.
hints: input().split() splits the line into a list of two words on the space between them.
parts = input().split(), then print(f"{parts[0][0]}.{parts[1][0]}.")

tasks.title: Simple password checker
tasks.brief:
A password is valid only if both of these are true:
- it is at least 8 characters long
- it contains at least one digit (0-9)

Read a password. Print Valid if both rules are met. Otherwise print Invalid.

For example, hello123 (8 characters, has a digit) is Valid. short1 (only 6 characters) is Invalid.
hints: Check the length with len(). To check for a digit, any(c.isdigit() for c in password) is True if at least one character in password is a digit.
pw = input(), has_digit = any(c.isdigit() for c in pw), print("Valid" if len(pw) >= 8 and has_digit else "Invalid")

tasks.title: Anagram check
tasks.brief:
Two words are anagrams if they use exactly the same letters, the same number of times each, just in a different order.

Read two words, each already lowercase with no spaces. Print Anagram if they are anagrams of each other. Otherwise print Not anagram.

For example, listen and silent are anagrams.
hints: sorted() works on a string too, and puts its characters in order - two anagrams sort to exactly the same sequence of letters.
a = input(), b = input(), print("Anagram" if sorted(a) == sorted(b) else "Not anagram")
